title: How to Think About Competitors
subtitle: Categories, tiers, and the do’s and don’ts
description: A working reference for Grace Hill marketing, sales, and product teams building and using competitive intelligence — including an audit of what we already have.

readThisFirst.title: Read this first
points: The frameworks in this document are durable. The competitor names and market facts are a snapshot compiled from public sources and our own two systems in August 2026 — a starting point for the categorization exercise, not a validated competitive map.

Sections 3 and 7 are an audit of our existing Jira competitor register and Drive battlecard library, and they are direct. That is deliberate: the gaps are specific, most of them are cheap to close, and several of the assets are already better than the systems around them.
Before anything here is used in customer-facing material, validate the specifics against CRM competitor fields and win/loss records.

foundationalQuestion.question: “What would our customers do if Grace Hill didn’t exist?”
foundationalQuestion.explanation: That single question surfaces the whole picture at once — rival vendors, the platforms that bundle a version of what we sell, and the spreadsheet, binder, or in-house trainer the buyer is using right now. Dunford calls the full set the customer’s competitive alternatives.

categories.name: Direct competitors
categories.test: Same solution, same buyer, same budget line. Shows up on the shortlist.
categories.demands: A value wedge and a battlecard.
categories.detail: Same solution category, same buyer, same budget line. These appear on real shortlists and in win/loss records. At Grace Hill they differ sharply by solution — some of our lines face two credible rivals, others face seventeen.

dos.headline: Let the buyer’s shortlist define who counts as direct.
dos.detail: If a vendor rarely lands on a shortlist, it is not a competitor you need to position against — regardless of how often it comes up internally.

dos.headline: Build a value wedge of two or three differentiators matched to that buyer’s stated priorities.
dos.detail: The intersection where our capability meets a need the rival can’t serve. Not a full feature parade.

donts.headline: Don’t maintain a direct-competitor list built from leadership opinion.
donts.detail: Companies routinely mis-state why they win and lose. Win/loss interviews and CRM competitor fields are the only reliable input — our own register has 36 Training records and one logged Training loss.

donts.headline: Don’t assume our own acquisitions are still competitors.
donts.detail: Edge2Learn and Ellis Partners are Grace Hill companies. Naming them as rivals in a deck is an unforced error — and it happens.

categories.name: Indirect competitors — the bundling platforms
categories.test: Solves the same job in a different shape — usually bundled inside something the buyer already owns.
categories.detail: These solve the same underlying job through a different product shape, usually as a module inside a system the customer already pays for. For Grace Hill this is the structurally important category, because it is where our whole go-to-market argument is decided.

dos.headline: Own the specialist lane explicitly.
dos.detail: Depth, currency, and regulatory maintenance of the content — not platform features — are what a bundled module cannot match.

dos.headline: Ask what the buyer will actually do with the bundled module.
dos.detail: “Included” and “used” are different things. An unused module is closer to status quo than to a competitor.

donts.headline: Don’t argue platform breadth against a platform.
donts.detail: That is their ground. Ours is the depth of the multifamily-specific library and the benchmark data behind it.

donts.headline: Don’t treat the bundle as a pricing problem.
donts.detail: Framing it as “we cost more than free” concedes the argument. Frame it as what a generic module costs in compliance exposure and staff time.

callout.title: The shape of the fight
callout.body: Grace Hill sells seven-plus specialist solutions. Yardi, RealPage, Entrata, Inhabit, and AppFolio bundle a version of several of them into a property management system the customer is already paying for.  The buyer’s question is therefore not “Is Grace Hill better?” It is “Is Grace Hill better enough to justify managing another vendor?” Every indirect-competitor conversation has to answer that second question, not the first.

categories.name: Replacement threats
categories.test: Makes the category itself unnecessary rather than competing inside it.
categories.demands: A roadmap and strategy conversation, not a card.
categories.detail: These do not compete inside the category — they make it unnecessary. They move more slowly than direct competition and matter more.

dos.headline: Route replacement threats to product and strategy, not to sales enablement.
dos.detail: There is no talk track that solves a category becoming obsolete.

dos.headline: Watch where churned customers actually go.
dos.detail: Churn destination is the earliest reliable signal that a replacement is real rather than theoretical.

donts.headline: Don’t confuse a replacement threat with a feature gap.
donts.detail: Responding to a structural shift by shipping parity features spends the budget and loses the ground anyway.

categories.name: Potential competitors — the watchlist
categories.test: Could enter, hasn’t yet. Not on buyer shortlists today.
categories.detail: Companies with the resources, customer base, or adjacency to enter, but who have not. In Grace Hill’s landscape: AI leasing platforms expanding their footprint, HR suites that could add multifamily-specific content to an existing LMS module, and platform data layers being assembled through acquisition.

dos.headline: Watch entry signals rather than features.
dos.detail: Job postings in our domain, acquisitions, executive statements about expansion, and feature creep are the leading indicators.

dos.headline: Keep the watchlist cheap.
dos.detail: Disruption does come from the fringes, so zero coverage is wrong — but a low-cost semi-annual scan is the right level of investment.

donts.headline: Don’t build enablement for a company sales has never encountered.
donts.detail: It produces content nobody uses and dilutes the positioning of the cards that matter.

callout.title: Dunford’s phantom competitor rule
callout.body: “You’re watering down your positioning by trying to position against them.”  This is the most-ignored discipline in competitive intelligence. If a company is not on real buyer shortlists, it does not get a battlecard, a comparison page, or a slide. It gets a line on a watchlist reviewed twice a year. A watchlist entry is a complete and legitimate answer.

categories.name: The status quo — our largest competitor
categories.test: The buyer does nothing new — manual process, an already-paid-for tool, free resources, or inertia.
categories.demands: A case for change. Usually our largest single loss category.
categories.detail: Dunford puts no-decision losses at 20–30% of enterprise deals. The JOLT Effect, analyzing 2.5 million recorded sales conversations, puts it at 40–60% of lost deals. The definitions differ, so cite the range rather than a single number — but under any measure, doing nothing beats every named vendor combined.  In Grace Hill’s market the status quo takes four distinct forms, and they need different responses.

dos.headline: Track “no decision” as a named competitor in the CRM.
dos.detail: If the competitor field only accepts vendor names, our biggest loss category is invisible in every report we run.

dos.headline: Build a status-quo battlecard before the fourth vendor battlecard.
dos.detail: We have exactly one — Paper-in-Binders, in Policies — and on argument quality it is the strongest card in the library. Replicate it per solution line, since the status quo differs by line.

dos.headline: Offer a recommendation rather than a neutral menu.
dos.detail: Dunford cites research showing win rates improved substantially when vendors proactively said what the prospect should do.

dos.headline: Take risk off the table when a buyer is hesitating.
dos.detail: Phased rollout, pilot scope, clear exit — these outperform escalating ROI claims once indecision has set in.

donts.headline: Don’t double down on cost-of-inaction messaging when a buyer stalls late in a cycle.
donts.detail: The JOLT data is unambiguous: this is the single most common and most damaging reflex in competitive selling.

donts.headline: Don’t sell a distant future-state vision to a hesitating buyer.
donts.detail: Dunford: orienting the story around a future market vision gives buyers more reasons to delay.

donts.headline: Don’t let “closed lost — other” absorb no-decision deals.
donts.detail: It is the single easiest fix in the whole program and it unlocks accurate win/loss reporting.

callout.title: The counterintuitive finding worth internalizing
callout.body: The JOLT research found that 73% of reps respond to buyer hesitation by pushing harder on the cost of inaction — and that doing so increased the likelihood of losing the deal by 84%. The reason is that most no-decision losses are not caused by contentment with the current state. They are caused by fear of making a bad choice.

categories.name: Partner-competitors
categories.test: A partner whose offering also draws from a budget we sell into.
categories.demands: Relationship management, not a competitive play.
categories.detail: This category is not in the standard taxonomy, but Grace Hill needs it. Some of the companies we partner with also draw from budgets we sell into. The risk is not that a partner is secretly a competitor — it is that the ambiguity gets resolved badly and locally, when a rep improvises a competitive framing in a live deal or a marketer builds a comparison page against a company whose logo is on our platform. Route any question about budget overlap with a partner to the partnership owner before using competitive language.

dos.headline: Name the partner-competitors explicitly and say what the rule is.
dos.detail: Ambiguity is what causes the damage. A one-line rule per relationship prevents improvisation in the field.

dos.headline: Route budget-overlap questions to the partnership owner.
dos.detail: These are relationship decisions with contract implications, not battlecard content.

donts.headline: Don’t build competitive enablement against a partner.
donts.detail: It will leak. Assume anything written internally reaches the partner eventually.

donts.headline: Don’t pretend the overlap doesn’t exist either.
donts.detail: Reps encounter it in real deals. Unacknowledged overlap produces worse improvisation than an acknowledged one.

whyMoreThanOneCompetitiveSet.explanation: Most companies have one competitive landscape. Grace Hill has several. We sell Training, Policies, Surveys, Mystery Shopping, Reputation Management, Realync virtual leasing, and HelloData® market intelligence — to overlapping but not identical buyers, against a different set of alternatives in each line. HelloData® competes with CoStar and Yardi Matrix for an underwriting and asset-management audience. Policies competes with a three-ring binder in SharePoint. Those are not the same fight, and a single flat competitor list flattens the difference.
rules: Maintain one competitive set per solution line, plus one portfolio-level set for PerformanceHQ. A rep selling Training and a rep selling HelloData® need different cards.

Categorize before you tier. Knowing what kind of alternative you are facing determines the response. A direct rival calls for a value wedge; the status quo calls for a case for change; a bundling platform calls for a specialist argument. Getting the category wrong means bringing the wrong play.

statusQuoForms.looksLike: An in-house trainer running sessions; a policy manual in SharePoint with acknowledgment tracked by email; comp shops phoned in and compiled in Excel; regional managers doing their own spot-checks
statusQuoForms.counter: Quantify the hidden cost — hours, error rate, inconsistency across properties, and compliance exposure. Make the invisible expense visible.

statusQuoForms.looksLike: An LMS module bundled in Paylocity or Paycom; reporting inside the PMS; free public review dashboards
statusQuoForms.counter: Separate platform from content. They own a delivery mechanism; the question is what goes in it, and whether it is multifamily-specific and current.

statusQuoForms.looksLike: NAA and NAAEI member education; local affiliate offerings; Multifamily Insiders webinars; free state fair-housing training (TDHCA, MSHDA and equivalents)
statusQuoForms.counter: Do not dismiss these — they are genuinely useful. Position on coverage, role-based assignment, tracking, and proof of completion across a portfolio.

statusQuoForms.looksLike: No owner, no budget line, no trigger event. Nothing is wrong enough today.
statusQuoForms.counter: This is the hardest one, and the most misdiagnosed. See below.

joltFinding.stat: The JOLT research found that 73% of reps respond to buyer hesitation by pushing harder on the cost of inaction — and that doing so increased the likelihood of losing the deal by 84%.
joltFinding.explanation: The reason is that most no-decision losses are not caused by contentment with the current state. They are caused by fear of making a bad choice. Those two things look identical from the outside and call for opposite responses.

twoStates.state: A buyer who has not yet decided to solve the problem
A buyer who is in-cycle and hesitating
twoStates.needs: Risk removed — a narrower set of options, an honest recommendation, a phased rollout, a proof of concept. More pressure at that moment makes it worse.

tiers.criteria: Appears in 30%+ of deals in that solution line. Cap at two or three per line.
tiers.gets: Full battlecard, real-time alerts, win/loss interviews, rep training, objection handling, quarterly refresh

tiers.criteria: Appears in a meaningful minority of opportunities
tiers.gets: Maintained one-page card, quarterly refresh, agreed positioning
High-level profile to reference as questions come up
A Jira record and monitoring. No enablement asset.

tiers.criteria: Present in every deal, by definition
tiers.gets: Treat as Tier 1 in every solution line. Its own card per line.

activityGuidance.intro: Gathering intel — the ethical and legal lines. The governing standard is the SCIP code of ethics. Two of its commitments do most of the work: disclose your identity and employer before conducting an interview, and provide honest analysis. The disclosure requirement is what rules out pretexting.

dos.headline: Use public sources freely.
dos.detail: Competitor websites and pricing pages, job postings, regulatory filings, patents, earnings calls, press, conference sessions attended under your own name, published reviews, and legitimately purchased products are all fair game.

dos.headline: Mine our own deals and our own people first.
dos.detail: The three most valuable records in the Jira register came from Slack messages from sales. Nothing produced by desk research comes close to them.

dos.headline: Label AI-generated research as AI-generated research.
dos.detail: Seven of our deepest records are LLM desk research, visible from the citation parameters. That is a legitimate starting point — but it arrived with our own side of the comparison unfilled, and it was filed as if finished.

dos.headline: Track competitor messaging, not just features.
dos.detail: Homepage copy, LinkedIn, ads, and conference talks reveal positioning shifts earlier than product changes do.

dos.headline: Brief reps on what not to disclose in demos, RFPs, and at conferences.
dos.detail: Competitors are running the same playbook against us.

donts.headline: Don’t misrepresent your identity or affiliation to obtain information.
donts.detail: Unethical everywhere and illegal in specific forms and jurisdictions. This rules out anonymous competitor trials under a false persona — sign up with a business email or don’t sign up.

donts.headline: Don’t induce anyone to breach an NDA or an employment obligation — including new hires from a competitor.
donts.detail: Trade secret misappropriation carries federal criminal exposure. Information assembled from the public domain carries none.

donts.headline: Don’t confuse collection with intelligence.
donts.detail: Without analysis you don’t have intelligence, you have a lot of information. Fifty-one link-only records is the shape that failure takes.

dos.headline: Write to a Fact → Impact → Act structure.
dos.detail: State the competitive fact, why it matters and when it applies, then the specific talk track, question, or next step. The LCP Media objection rebuttal already does this; nothing else in the library does.

dos.headline: Add owner, last-reviewed date, and review cadence to the face of every card.
dos.detail: None of our 20 cards carries any of the three. It is why a card citing a stock ticker retired in 2023 is still in the folder.

dos.headline: Add a Sources section and use it.
dos.detail: Two of twenty cards have one. Paper-in-Binders — the card that depends most on hard numbers — carries footnote markers pointing at nothing.

dos.headline: Convert every Weaknesses bullet into a question a rep can ask.
dos.detail: The raw material for trap-setting questions is already sitting in every card. The four best questions we have were written in an email and never promoted onto a card.

dos.headline: Take a position and make every claim specific and provable.
dos.detail: “The only ORM tool available with…” appears at least six times across the Reputation family. Superlatives that broad are easy for a competitor to disprove in front of a buyer.

dos.headline: Put cards where reps already work.
dos.detail: A separate Drive folder is a repository, not a workflow. Linking the card from the competitor’s record — and from the CRM competitor field — is the cheap version of this.

donts.headline: Don’t ship a feature-comparison spreadsheet.
donts.detail: It is the most common form of competitive content and the least used. Forrester goes as far as calling product-vs-product battlecards a relic of outdated selling.

donts.headline: Don’t build a card by copying a neighboring card.
donts.detail: This is exactly how the Reputation.com card became a Widewail card and how a SatisFacts rebuttal ended up inside a Widewail row. Start from the competitor, not from the nearest file.

donts.headline: Don’t anchor a card on price.
donts.detail: Positioning and outcomes hold up. Our price anchors currently range from 2020 to 2024, and one of them is aimed at a competitor explicitly flagged as willing to price-match.

donts.headline: Don’t let a card go stale.
donts.detail: Once a rep is corrected by a prospect using our own material, they stop trusting the whole system — not just that slide. Retire what we cannot maintain.

activityGuidance.activity: Talking about competitors in a live deal

dos.headline: Raise differentiation early.
dos.detail: Competitive selling is like shaping wet clay — wait until the evaluation criteria have set and you cannot move them.

dos.headline: Acknowledge genuine strengths factually, then pivot.
dos.detail: Paper-in-Binders does this better than any card we have: it concedes four real advantages of the binder before naming eight failures. Dismissiveness reads as insecurity; steelmanning reads as confidence.

dos.headline: Match the response to the type of claim.
dos.detail: Blatantly false or outdated → address directly with third-party proof. Partially true → concede the true part and reframe. True but irrelevant, or simply true → redirect to our differentiators.

dos.headline: Set traps as positive statements about us, not negatives about them.
dos.detail: “Our customers value that our fair housing content is state-approved and updated as regulation changes” beats “their content is generic.”

dos.headline: Walk the buyer through the available approaches — including doing nothing — with honest pros and cons, then recommend.
dos.detail: Buyers are experts in pain; we are experts in solutions. The job is to teach them how to buy.

dos.headline: Disqualify honestly when we are not the right fit.
dos.detail: It protects the relationship, the forecast, and the renewal we would otherwise have lost in year two.

donts.headline: Don’t trash-talk a competitor.
donts.detail: It diminishes our professionalism, invites retaliation, and insults the buyer’s judgment for having shortlisted them.

donts.headline: Don’t make specific factual claims about a competitor’s product.
donts.detail: Anytime you state a specific there is a real risk you are wrong. Absolute negatives — “they have no X” — are the highest-risk form.

donts.headline: Don’t name competitors the prospect hasn’t mentioned.
donts.detail: Dunford: nine times out of ten it is best not to name a competitor unless you are certain the buyer has heard of them. Introducing new alternatives gives them new reasons to delay.

donts.headline: Don’t try to obscure the playing field.
donts.detail: A tactic some CI guidance endorses. The indecision research says the opposite: confusion sends buyers to the lowest-risk option, which is no decision. Clarity wins.

dos.headline: Give the program a single named owner.
dos.detail: No defined ownership and no update schedule is the standard reason intelligence goes stale — and the reason two systems can hold complementary halves of the same answer for two years.

dos.headline: Close the loop from register to card.
dos.detail: Every Tier 1 and Tier 2 record should link to its battlecard, and every battlecard should link back. Today that link exists once, on J Turner.

dos.headline: Keep the Slack-to-register channel alive and visible.
dos.detail: It produced our three best records and then went quiet. A named channel, a weekly triage, and visible credit for contributions is all it takes.

dos.headline: Get intel to sales on a weekly clock.
dos.detail: Cadence is among the strongest predictors of revenue impact — ahead of tooling or presentation quality.

dos.headline: Secure an executive sponsor inside sales and track metrics.
dos.detail: Programs with tracked metrics and sales-side sponsorship are several times more likely to demonstrably drive revenue.

dos.headline: Run win/loss as third-party buyer interviews, not surveys.
dos.detail: Decision-makers participate in interviews far more often than surveys and give far more time. Interview wins and no-decisions too, not just losses.

dos.headline: Harvest churn and save threads systematically.
dos.detail: The single most honest piece of competitive content we own is a customer telling us why they left. It is sitting in a folder as an email, not in any card.

donts.headline: Don’t treat rep-reported loss reasons as fact.
donts.detail: Reps skew toward external causes — price, product gaps — over execution issues, and prospects don’t tell sellers everything. Verify rather than accept.

donts.headline: Don’t let CI live only inside product marketing.
donts.detail: It should feed pricing, product, and strategy — not just sales enablement. The register sits in the product discovery project; the cards sit in a marketing folder. Neither reaches the other.

donts.headline: Don’t treat a bulk field update as maintenance.
donts.detail: Sixty-two records updated on one day reads as a healthy, current register in every report. It isn’t one.

dos.headline: Tier on deal frequency, drawn from data.
dos.detail: Benchmark data shows the median company tracks around 32 competitors. We track 65. Tracking is cheap; deep enablement is not. Scale effort inversely down the tiers.

dos.headline: Re-tier at least annually and drop what has gone quiet.
dos.detail: Tiers drift. A Tier 3 competitor becoming Tier 1 is exactly the signal a CI program exists to catch.

donts.headline: Don’t deeply track eight to fifteen competitors per line.
donts.detail: It produces shallow intelligence on all of them and reliable intelligence on none. Thirty-six Training records with no prose in any of them is the current illustration.

donts.headline: Don’t assume tracked count should equal battlecard count.
donts.detail: Both patterns exist across industries. Pick deliberately rather than by default.

whereSourcesDisagree.positions: Dunford says ignore anyone off the buyer shortlist; CI practitioners warn against fringe blindness.
whereSourcesDisagree.reconciliation: Reconcile by separating positioning scope (shortlist only) from monitoring scope (a cheap watchlist — which is what most of our 65 records should be).

whereSourcesDisagree.positions: Some battlecard guidance advises obscuring the playing field on defense. Dunford, Forrester, and the indecision research all point the other way.
whereSourcesDisagree.reconciliation: The clarity position has better empirical support.

whereSourcesDisagree.positions: SCIP-aligned sources require disclosure of identity; some marketing sources endorse undetected persona-based shopping.
whereSourcesDisagree.reconciliation: These are irreconcilable — pick a policy explicitly rather than leaving it to individual judgment.
Different samples and definitions. Cite the range.
